passage:
I was third in the line at the bakery counter when I saw it. A man walked up and stood at the front, right beside the register. A woman in a green scarf, Gargi, turned to him with a smile and said, “Sorry to jump in, but the queue begins over by the door.”
He frowned. “I’m only buying one thing.”
“Of course,” she said, still pleasant. “Most of us are, though. It’s just past the door.”
For a second I thought he would snap. Instead he shrugged, muttered something, and walked to the end. Gargi turned back to the counter and did not look smug. I’m Sharmila, and I’m not sure whether she was nervous, but her voice never rose.

qa.q: What did Gargi say to the man at the front?
qa.a: Gargi said, “Sorry to jump in, but the queue begins over by the door.”

qa.q: What might Gargi have been feeling as she spoke to the man?
qa.a: Gargi may have felt a little nervous but determined to be fair, though Sharmila cannot know for sure; the passage only shows a pleasant, steady voice that never rose.

qa.q: What helped Gargi's request work, according to what Sharmila saw?
qa.a: Gargi smiled, stayed pleasant and repeated the point with no heat. She also did not gloat once the man had walked to the end.

qa.q: How might the man have experienced being sent to the end of the queue?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or defensive at being pointed out, which fits his frown and excuse, but the pleasant tone let him shrug and walk to the end without a scene.

grounding: Shows an observer describing a woman politely saying where the line starts, with calm friendly firmness that works.

passage:
Tuesday, post office. Kamal was fifth in the line when a man stepped up to the window ahead of everyone. “Hi, the queue starts by the door,” Kamal said, smiling. The man nodded, said “Oh, sorry,” and went to the end.
Friday. Another man pushed in. Kamal repeated the same words. This time the man snapped, “Who made you the boss?” The woman ahead of Kamal went quiet, and the others looked away. Kamal’s heart thumped. He said, “Fair enough,” shrugged, and let it go rather than arguing.
Next Monday. Vinita, who had slid in near the front, saw Kamal glance at her. “Sorry, I didn’t see the line,” she said, and stepped back.

qa.q: Which day did the second man snap at Kamal?
qa.a: The second man snapped at Kamal on Friday.

qa.q: What was Kamal probably feeling when his heart thumped on Friday?
qa.a: Kamal was likely nervous and unsure, since the man turned hostile and no one spoke up. His quick, calm reply suggests he did not want the moment to grow into a fight.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Kamal to let it go on Friday?
qa.a: The man had turned hostile, and pushing further could have made things worse. Kamal had already said the line clearly, and it was not worth a quarrel.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when Kamal glanced at her on Monday?
qa.a: Vinita may have felt caught out and slightly embarrassed, which is why she apologised and stepped back at once.

grounding: Shows a person calmly saying where the line starts over several days, succeeding when friendly and letting it go when a man turns hostile.

passage: Nikita, you want to know how to handle line-cutters without a fight? Your Ritu masi has had practice. In 1994 I worked at the post office counter in Jaipur. Every pension day, someone tried to slip in. I learned to smile and say, 'Excuse me, uncle, the line starts at the door. You'll be served soon, promise.' Most people went back, a bit sheepish. One day a man shouted at me, red-faced, that he was an important person. The people in line were getting tense. I didn't argue. I served him quickly, and then apologised to the next woman in line for the wait. Later my boss asked why I'd given in. I said, 'Because a fight in a queue helps nobody.'

qa.q: What did Ritu masi say to line-cutters?
qa.a: 'Excuse me, uncle, the line starts at the door. You'll be served soon, promise.'

qa.q: How might the people in line have felt when the man shouted?
qa.a: Tense and uneasy, worried the shouting would turn into a fight.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows when to let it go?
qa.a: When the man turned hostile, Ritu served him quickly instead of arguing, then apologised to the next woman, keeping everyone safe.

qa.q: How might the woman next in line have felt after Ritu's apology?
qa.a: Probably still annoyed at the man but respected and less upset, since Ritu acknowledged her wait.

grounding: An aunt recalls enforcing a queue with calm, friendly firmness, and letting it go when a man turned hostile.

passage: The line for the free eye camp at the community hall had been growing since dawn, and by noon the heat was brutal. Chetan, a volunteer, was handing out tokens at the door. A young man, Lokesh, walked past thirty elderly people and held out his hand for a token. 'For my grandmother, she's in the auto.' Chetan kept his voice warm. 'Excuse me, bhai, the line starts at the gate. If she can't stand, bring her to the shade and we'll give her a priority token.' Lokesh hesitated, then went to fetch her. She really was frail, and Chetan seated her first. Ten minutes later another man tried the same trick and began shouting when stopped. Chetan let him pass rather than start a fight, and made a note to tell the camp lead.

qa.q: What did Chetan offer Lokesh's grandmother?
qa.a: A priority token, if she was brought to the shade.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have felt when Chetan kindly stopped him?
qa.a: A bit caught out and hesitant, but also relieved to be offered a fair way for his grandmother.

qa.q: How did Chetan balance firmness and safety?
qa.a: He was warm and clear with Lokesh, offering a fair option, but when the second man turned hostile, Chetan let it go and reported it instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might the thirty elderly people in line feel watching this?
qa.a: Reassured that the line mattered, and perhaps uneasy when the shouting man pushed through.

grounding: A volunteer enforces a queue in the heat with calm, friendly firmness, and lets it go when a man turns hostile.

passage: At the busy bakery counter in Lajpat Nagar, the queue was eight deep when Pradeep, phone to his ear, strode to the front and asked for a birthday cake. Alka, next in line, felt a familiar flash of irritation. She kept her voice light. 'Sorry, the queue's that way, just behind the aunty in green.' Pradeep looked round, surprised. 'Oh. Sorry, I didn't see. My daughter's party starts in twenty minutes.' 'Then you'd better hurry,' Alka said, smiling. 'It moves fast.' He laughed and went to the back. The aunty in green said to Alka, 'I'd have shouted.' Alka shrugged. 'Shouting takes longer.' Pradeep got his cake eleven minutes later and waved at her on the way out.

qa.q: How long until Pradeep's daughter's party?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Alka feel when Pradeep strode to the front?
qa.a: A familiar flash of irritation, which she chose to cover with a light voice.

qa.q: What made Alka's approach work?
qa.a: Calm, friendly firmness: pointing to where the queue is, smiling and joking, so Pradeep moved back without a fight.

qa.q: How might the aunty in green see Alka's approach?
qa.a: She would have shouted, so she seems surprised and perhaps impressed that a calm word worked.

grounding: A woman politely enforces a bakery queue with calm, friendly firmness, and it works.

passage:
"Excuse me," Elizabeth said, smiling, as Kashish stepped in front of her at the bakery counter. "The queue begins back there, by the door."
Kashish turned, surprised. "Oh! Does it? I thought this was the pickup counter."
"Easy to miss. The sign's tiny."
"Sorry, sorry." Kashish went to the back. The old man behind Elizabeth chuckled. "Nicely done."
Ten minutes later a man in a gym vest walked straight to the till. "Sorry, the queue begins by the door," Elizabeth said, same tone.
"Mind your own business," he snapped.
The cashier glanced at her. Elizabeth shrugged. "Fine. Go ahead."
"You're letting him?" whispered the old man.
"It's two croissants," Elizabeth said. "Not worth a fight."
From the back of the line, Kashish laughed. "You were right the first time, though."

qa.q: Where does the queue begin, according to Elizabeth?
qa.a: The queue begins back there, by the door.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth let the man in the gym vest go ahead?
qa.a: She stayed calm but was cautious; once he turned hostile, she felt a fight over two croissants was not worth it.

qa.q: What made Elizabeth's first request work with Kashish?
qa.a: She smiled, said where the queue begins without accusing, and offered an easy reason for the mistake.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt on being told about the line?
qa.a: Kashish was surprised and a little embarrassed but not humiliated, since the tone was friendly, so moving to the back felt easy.

grounding: Shows a person calmly and warmly enforcing a queue, which works, and letting it go when someone turns hostile.
